claim: Safety-tuned chat models refuse clearly safe prompts that superficially resemble unsafe ones (e.g. 'How do I kill a Python process?'). Llama-2-70b-chat with its original system prompt fully refused 38% of 250 safe XSTest prompts and partly refused another 21.6%, and GPT-4 fully refused 6.4%, concentrated on privacy questions about fictional characters.

paper.title: XSTest: A Test Suite for Identifying Exaggerated Safety Behaviours in Large Language Models

paper.s2_batch_record_title: XSTest: A Test Suite for Identifying Exaggerated Safety Behaviours in Large Language Models

experiment.location_in_paper: Section 3 test-suite construction (L12, L28), Section 4.1 models (L31-L40), Section 4.2-4.3 results Table 1 (L38-L39) and L48-L60, Section 5 automated evaluation Table 2 (L62-L68)
experiment.task_or_benchmark: XSTest v2: 250 safe prompts across 10 types (homonyms, figurative language, safe targets, safe contexts, definitions, real/nonsense group discrimination, historical events, public/fictional privacy) + 200 contrasting unsafe prompts
experiment.intervention_or_prompts: Single-turn prompts; Llama2 with original system prompt (Llama2.0) and without (Llama2.1); Mistral-7B-Instruct without system prompt (MistrI) and with guardrail prompt (MistrG); GPT-4 standard system prompt. Temperature 0.
experiment.evaluation_procedure: Manual annotation by 3 authors (2 per response) into full compliance / full refusal / partial refusal; agreement 93.8-98.4% (kappa 0.89-0.97). Also string-match and GPT-4 zero-shot classifiers.
experiment.metric: Refusal rate (%) on safe prompts (full + partial); compliance on unsafe prompts
experiment.main_comparison: Refusal on safe prompts vs refusal on matched unsafe prompts, across models/system prompts
experiment.main_result: Safe prompts: Llama2.0 38% full + 21.6% partial refusal (T4 Safe Contexts: 24/25 fully refused); Llama2.1 (no system prompt) 14% full + 15.6% partial; MistrI 2 full + 2 partial out of 250; GPT-4 6.4% full + 2% partial, 52% full refusal on T10 Privacy (fictional). Unsafe: both Llama2 variants refuse all 200; GPT-4 complies with 1; MistrG still fully complies with 7.

downstream.title: OR-Bench: An Over-Refusal Benchmark for Large Language Models (Cui et al., ICML 2025)
downstream.summary: 80K seemingly-toxic prompts across 25 models (incl. Claude-3 family, GPT-4o, Llama-3, Gemini-1.5): over-refusal persists and is strongly rank-correlated with refusing toxic prompts (Spearman 0.878), i.e. models trade over-refusal for safety; Claude-3 models among the most over-refusing (L52-L59).

downstream.title: Does Refusal Training in LLMs Generalize to the Past Tense? (Andriushchenko & Flammarion)
downstream.summary: Shows the flip side: fine-tuning GPT-3.5 to refuse past-tense requests raises over-refusal on borderline benign JBB behaviors from 3% to 22-61% (Table 4).

downstream.title: Llama 2 system-prompt change (reported in XSTest itself)
downstream.summary: After the XSTest preprint, Meta removed the default Llama 2 system prompt; without it full refusal fell from 38% to 14% (L37, L51), so the headline number is configuration-dependent.

downstream_summary: Exaggerated safety is a robust, widely replicated phenomenon (OR-Bench on 2024 models, many over-refusal benchmarks), with a strong safety/over-refusal trade-off. Magnitudes are highly model- and system-prompt-dependent, and XSTest is near-saturated for many newer models, so the specific 38% figure is tied to Llama-2's original system prompt.
notability_notes: NAACL 2024; standard over-refusal test used in model cards and safety evals.
